mainTopic: Is drinking included in 'eating' for a שבועה? Proofs from פסוקים and the משנה, and why naming each bread separately makes separate oaths.
overview: The גמרא wants to show that drinking counts as a kind of eating, which matters for someone who swears a שבועה not to eat. First it brings proofs from פסוקים that use the word 'ואכלת' for wine. It pushes back that the wine might have been eaten in a cooked dish (אניגרון), or that שכר might mean intoxicating figs. In the end a גזירה שוה from נזיר shows that שכר means wine. Then רבא brings a proof from the משנה: one who swore not to eat and then ate and drank is liable only once. אביי challenges him from the סיפא. The גמרא answers that saying 'and I will not drink' shows the person meant plain eating only. רב אשי offers another proof from the משנה, but it is pushed away. Finally the גמרא asks why naming each kind of bread creates separate oaths, and it tries several shorter wordings the person could have used.

steps.title: Wine is called 'eating' in the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The proof finishes: תירוש is wine, and the פסוק uses the word 'ואכלת' for it, so drinking is a kind of eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: And תירוש means wine, and the פסוק says about it, 'And you shall eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof that started just before this section. The פסוק uses the word 'eat' about wine, which is something you drink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists תירוש, which is wine, among the things of מעשר שני and says 'ואכלת', 'you shall eat.' Wine is normally drunk. So if the תורה calls having wine 'eating,' then drinking falls under eating.

keyTerms.meaning: A word the פסוק uses for wine

phrases.english: And tirosh is wine,
phrases.notes: This is the תירוש from the פסוק quoted just before this section (דברים 14:23).

phrases.english: and it is written: 'And you shall eat.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a proof that began before this section.
steps.raayaObject: שתייה בכלל אכילה: drinking counts as eating.

steps.title: Maybe the wine was eaten in a cooked dish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. Maybe the wine was mixed into a beet dish called אניגרון, so it really was eaten. רבה בר שמואל defines the dish.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the פסוק means wine eaten through אניגרון? As רבה בר שמואל said: אניגרון is a beet broth, and אכסיגרון is a broth of all kinds of cooked vegetables.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof. It suggests the wine in the פסוק was not drunk but cooked into a food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof only works if the wine in the פסוק was drunk. If the wine was part of a cooked dish like אניגרון, then 'ואכלת' is simply about eating food. In that case the פסוק teaches nothing about drinking. רבה בר שמואל's words show that such a dish really existed.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe: an opening for a pushback
A cooked beet broth that wine was mixed into
A broth made from all kinds of cooked vegetables

steps.confusionAlert: The pushback does not say wine is not a drink. It only says this פסוק might be talking about wine that was eaten in food, so the proof does not work.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is by means of anigeron?
phrases.notes: In other words, maybe the wine was eaten as part of a cooked dish, not drunk.

phrases.english: As Rabba bar Shmuel said:
Anigeron is beet broth,
aksigeron is the broth of all cooked vegetables.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 1 by reading the פסוק a different way.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from תירוש alone. The idea that drinking counts as eating is not itself rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wine could have been eaten inside a cooked dish (אניגרון), so 'ואכלת' may be about real eating.

steps.title: A new proof from the מעשר שני money פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב brings a different פסוק. It lists יין among the things you may buy with מעשר שני money, and then says 'ואכלת.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אחא בר יעקב said: the proof is from here: 'And you shall spend the money on whatever your soul desires, on cattle, sheep, wine, and strong drink.' יין is wine, and it says 'And you shall eat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The first proof was pushed away, so רב אחא בר יעקב offers a new פסוק to prove that drinking counts as eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק is about food bought with מעשר שני money. It openly names יין and שכר, which are drinks, and then says 'ואכלת.' The idea is the same as before: wine is called 'eaten.' But here the drinks are named outright alongside the word 'ואכלת.'

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: the earlier proof is dropped and a new one begins

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב, מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: from here:
'And you shall spend the money on all
that your soul desires,
on cattle, and on sheep, and on wine, and on strong drink';
yayin is wine,
and it is written: 'And you shall eat.'
phrases.notes: The word 'ואכלת' comes later in the same פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב, מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof that was rejected in Step 2 with a new פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: שתייה בכלל אכילה: drinking counts as eating.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 14:26: יין and שכר are listed, together with 'ואכלת'.

steps.title: The same pushback hits the new proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this פסוק too might mean wine eaten in an אניגרון dish.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe here too it means by means of אניגרון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the same pushback against רב אחא בר יעקב's proof. Maybe this wine was also eaten in a cooked dish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming יין outright does not settle it. Wine bought with מעשר שני money could still be cooked into אניגרון and eaten. So the new proof has the same weakness as the first, and the search for a proof goes on.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too: the same argument used again

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs from wine (תירוש and יין) are pushed away for the same reason: the wine might have been eaten inside a cooked dish (אניגרון), not drunk. So the פסוק calling it 'eating' does not yet prove that drinking counts as eating.

phrases.english: But perhaps here too
it is by means of anigeron?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא הָכָא נָמֵי עַל יְדֵי אֲנִיגְרוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the pushback from Step 2 against the new proof in Step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רב אחא בר יעקב's proof from the מעשר שני money פסוק.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The יין in the פסוק could also have been eaten inside a cooked dish, so 'ואכלת' does not prove anything about drinking.

steps.title: The verse says 'strong drink,' so it must be something intoxicating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the אניגרון idea. The פסוק says שכר, which means something that makes a person drunk, and a cooked dish does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'שכר' (strong drink), meaning something that makes you drunk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אחא בר יעקב's proof against the challenge in step 4. Wine cooked into a beet dish would not make anyone drunk, but the פסוק talks about שכר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said the wine in the פסוק might have been eaten inside an אניגרון dish. Here the גמרא points to the word שכר in the same פסוק, which means an intoxicating drink. A cooked dish does not intoxicate, so the פסוק must mean actual drinking, and it still says 'ואכלת.'

keyTerms.meaning: Strong drink, something that makes a person drunk

phrases.english: "Strong drink" is written,
phrases.notes: This is the same מעשר שני פסוק from step 3 (דברים 14:26), which says 'ביין ובשכר.'

phrases.english: meaning something that intoxicates.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the אניגרון answer from step 4 and brings back רב אחא בר יעקב's proof.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading a word in the פסוק closely
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wine in the פסוק might have been eaten in a cooked dish.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק says שכר, which means something intoxicating, so it is talking about real drinking.

steps.title: Maybe 'strong drink' means intoxicating pressed figs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that שכר could mean a food that intoxicates, like pressed figs from קעילה. Then it would really be eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe it means pressed figs from קעילה? As a ברייתא teaches: if a כהן ate pressed figs from קעילה, or drank honey and milk, and then entered the מקדש and did the עבודה, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 5. Some foods can make you drunk too, so שכר might mean an intoxicating food and not a drink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 assumed only a drink can intoxicate. The ברייתא shows that pressed figs from קעילה can make a כהן drunk enough to be liable for doing עבודה. If the פסוק's שכר means figs, then 'ואכלת' is about real eating, and the proof is gone again.

keyTerms.meaning: Pressed figs from the town of קעילה, known to intoxicate
And he performed the service (עבודה) in the מקדש

phrases.english: But maybe it means pressed figs from Ke'ila?
As it is taught:
If he ate pressed figs from Ke'ila
phrases.notes: This is talking about a כהן, who may not serve in the מקדש while drunk.

phrases.english: or drank honey and milk,
and entered the Temple and served, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 5's claim that שכר must be a drink.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the word שכר proves the פסוק means drinking.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Some foods intoxicate too, so שכר could mean an intoxicating food that is really eaten.

steps.title: Learning 'strong drink' from נזיר: it means wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns from a גזירה שוה with נזיר that שכר means wine. So the proof that drinking is called eating stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we learn the word 'שכר' here from the word 'שכר' in נזיר. Just as there it means wine, here too it means wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 6 with a גזירה שוה. The same word שכר appears in the פרשה of נזיר, and there it means wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said שכר might mean intoxicating figs. Since the word שכר in נזיר clearly means a kind of wine, it carries the same meaning in the מעשר שני פסוק. That makes it a drink, and the פסוק still says 'ואכלת,' so drinking counts as eating.

keyTerms.meaning: Learning the meaning of a word from the same word in another פסוק
A person who vowed to stay away from wine and grape products
Just as there, so too here

steps.whatToRemember: With the גזירה שוה from נזיר, the proof holds: the פסוק calls drinking wine 'ואכלת,' so drinking is included in eating.

phrases.english: Rather, we learn
"strong drink" and "strong drink" from the nazirite;
just as there it means wine,
so too here it means wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the figs challenge from step 6 and brings back רב אחא בר יעקב's proof.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שכר might mean an intoxicating food like pressed figs.
steps.terutzMaskana: שכר means wine, as in נזיר, so the פסוק calls drinking 'eating.'

steps.title: רבא proves from the משנה that drinking is included in eating
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings support from the משנה. Someone swore not to eat, then ate and drank, and he is liable only once. That ruling is only needed if drinking counts as eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: We also learned this in our משנה. If someone said 'An oath that I will not eat,' and then ate and drank, he is liable for only one. This makes sense if drinking is included in eating, because then the תנא had to teach that it is only one. But if drinking is not included in eating, it would be like saying: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and he ate and did work. Would we need to be told that he is liable only once?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a new proof, this time from a משנה instead of a פסוק. He shows that the משנה's ruling only makes sense if drinking is a kind of eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that eating and drinking after 'I will not eat' brings only one חיוב. That ruling is only worth teaching if we might have thought drinking is a second, separate act of eating. If drinking had nothing to do with eating, the case would be as obvious as eating and then doing work, which no one would need to be told.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have learned this (in a משנה)
An oath that I will not eat
Included in the category of eating
It was necessary to teach us
It works well if you say

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying that drinking breaks the oath as a separate act. The point is the opposite: drinking is part of eating, so eating plus drinking adds up to one חיוב and not two.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that in the language of a שבועה, 'eating' includes drinking. That decides what a person forbids himself when he swears not to eat.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא, אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא:
phrases.english: Rava said: We too have also learned it:
"An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate and drank,
he is liable for only one.
phrases.notes: Only one קרבן, not one for eating and another for drinking.

phrases.english: It works well if you say
that drinking is included in eating;
then the tanna needed
to teach us that he is liable for only one.
But if you say
that drinking is not included in eating,
then it is like: "An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate and did work,
would it be necessary to teach us
that he is liable for only one?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, independent proof from the משנה, after the פסוק-based proof was settled.
steps.raayaObject: That drinking is included in eating.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: 'שבועה שלא אוכל' and he ate and drank, he is liable only once.

steps.title: אביי challenges רבא from the second half of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks: if drinking is included in eating, why does the סיפא make someone who swore not to eat and not to drink liable twice? The words 'I will not drink' should add nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: So you think drinking is part of eating? Look at the end of the משנה: 'An oath that I will not eat and I will not drink,' and he ate and drank, he is liable twice. If saying 'I will not eat' already forbade drinking, why is he liable for the words 'I will not drink'? If he had said 'I will not drink' twice, would he be liable twice?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's proof by pointing to the next case in the same משנה. That case seems to show that drinking is a separate thing from eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבא, 'I will not eat' already covers drinking. So adding 'I will not drink' should be like repeating the same oath, and a repeated oath does not take effect a second time. Yet the משנה says he is liable twice, which suggests the two words are separate.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather, what?' A way of asking 'So what are you saying?' before showing a problem
The later part of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: A שבועה on something already forbidden by an earlier שבועה does not take effect. That is why 'I will not drink' twice would only count once. אביי's whole question depends on this.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Rather, what, drinking is included in eating?!
Say the latter clause:
"An oath that I will not eat and that I will not drink,"
and he ate and drank, he is liable for two.
Since he said "that I will not eat",
drinking became forbidden to him;
when he said "that I will not drink", why is he liable?
If he had said "that I will not drink" two times,
would he be liable for two?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֶלָּא מַאי, שְׁתִיָּה בִּכְלַל אֲכִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's proof from the רישא by using the סיפא of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that שתיה is included in אכילה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'I will not eat' already forbids drinking, then 'I will not drink' is a repeated oath and should not make him liable a second time. But the סיפא says he is liable twice.

steps.title: רבא: the second case is where he said drinking first
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the סיפא is talking about someone who said 'I will not drink' first and then 'I will not eat.' Eating includes drinking, but drinking does not include eating, so both oaths take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: There, the case is where he said 'I will not drink' and then said 'I will not eat.' Drinking is included in eating, but eating is not included in drinking.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends his view by reading the סיפא as a case where drinking was mentioned first. That way each oath adds something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'eat' is wide and covers drinking, but the word 'drink' is narrow and does not cover eating. So 'I will not drink' forbids only drinks. Then 'I will not eat' still adds a new ban on food, which is why he is liable twice.

keyTerms.meaning: It is so / It is not so

phrases.english: He said to him:
There, it is where he said "that I will not drink",
and then said "that I will not eat";
for drinking is included in eating,
but eating is not included in drinking.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם דְּאָמַר שֶׁלֹּא אֶשְׁתֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge by redefining the case of the סיפא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case (the order of the words)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The סיפא is someone who said 'eat' first and then 'drink,' so the second word adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The סיפא is someone who said 'drink' first; the later 'eat' still adds food, so he is liable twice.

steps.title: Then the משנה should have taught the bigger case in the first half
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: according to רבא, someone who said 'I will not eat and I will not drink' in that order would be liable only once. If so, the רישא should have taught that case, and we would know the simpler case by קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said 'An oath that I will not eat and I will not drink,' and ate and drank, what, he is liable only once? If so, instead of the first clause teaching 'An oath that I will not eat' and he ate and drank, he is liable only once, let it teach 'An oath that I will not eat and I will not drink,' he is liable only once, and all the more so 'I will not eat' by itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's answer. If the eat-then-drink case gives only one liability, the משנה picked the weaker example to teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying both words makes it look more like two oaths, so 'only once' there is the bigger חידוש. A משנה usually teaches the case that tells us the most. Since it taught only 'I will not eat,' it seems the eat-and-drink case really gives two liabilities, against רבא's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a משנה

phrases.english: But if he said "an oath
that I will not eat and that I will not drink", and he ate and drank,
what, he is liable only once?
phrases.notes: That is what רבא's answer implies, since here 'eat' came first and already covered drinking.

phrases.english: If so, instead of teaching in the first clause:
"An oath that I will not eat" and he ate and drank
he is liable only once;
let it teach: "An oath that I will not eat and that I will not drink"
he is liable only once,
and all the more so "that I will not eat" by itself!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל אָמַר שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל וְשֶׁלֹּא אֶשְׁתֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in Step 10 by pointing out what it implies about the eat-then-drink case.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reading that the סיפא is a drink-then-eat case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If eat-then-drink gives only one liability, the רישא should have taught that stronger case, and we would know 'I will not eat' alone by קל וחומר. Since it didn't, the eat-then-drink case must give two.

steps.title: Saying 'and I will not drink' shows he meant plain eating
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the plain reading: the סיפא is eat-then-drink, and he is liable twice. That case is different, because by adding 'I will not drink' he showed that his word 'eat' meant only food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really it is as it is taught. Here it is different: since he said 'I will not eat' and then said 'I will not drink,' he revealed his intention that the eating he mentioned is plain eating alone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops רבא's change of order and gives a new answer that keeps the משנה as written. Drinking is normally part of eating, but this person's own words show he meant otherwise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually 'I will not eat' covers drinking too, as רבא proved from the רישא. But a person who goes on to say 'and I will not drink' shows he was using 'eat' in the narrow sense of food only. So each oath covers something different, and he is liable twice. רבא's main point still stands, and אביי's question from the סיפא is answered.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, it is just as it is taught

steps.whatToRemember: Normally 'I will not eat' includes drinking, so eating and drinking after that oath gives only one liability. But if he says 'I will not eat and I will not drink,' his own words show that 'eat' meant food only, so he is liable twice.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the meaning of a שבועה can depend on how the person worded the whole statement, not only on the usual meaning of each word.

phrases.english: Rather, really it is as it is taught;
phrases.notes: Keep the order the משנה uses, 'eat' first and then 'drink'; רבא's switched order is dropped.

phrases.english: and here it is different,
since he said "that I will not eat"
and then said "that I will not drink",
he revealed his intention
that this eating that he said
is plain eating alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 11, drops רבא's rereading, and answers אביי's original question from Step 9 differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case by the person's revealed intention
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since 'eat' includes drinking, the words 'I will not drink' are a repeated oath and add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: By adding 'I will not drink,' he showed that 'eat' meant food only, so both oaths take effect and he is liable twice, while drinking is still normally part of eating.

steps.title: רב אשי proves from the משנה that drinking counts as eating
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי points to the משנה: a person who swore 'I will not eat' is exempt only for drinks that are not drinkable. That means he would be liable for normal drinks, so 'eating' must include drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The משנה also shows this. It says: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and he ate foods not fit to eat, or drank drinks not fit to drink, he is exempt. So if they were fit, he would be liable. But why? He only said 'an oath that I will not eat'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings a new proof, from a close reading of the משנה, that drinking is included in 'eating.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts him because the drinks were undrinkable. That suggests that if the drinks were drinkable, he would be liable. His oath only mentioned eating, so drinking must be part of 'eating.'

keyTerms.meaning: It is precise; a careful reading of the wording proves the point
Fit for eating, normal edible food
Liable, here to bring a קרבן
And why? Asks for the reason behind a ruling

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
The mishna is also precise on this point:
"An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate foods that are not fit for eating,

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁתָה מַשְׁקִין שֶׁאֵין רְאוּיִן לִשְׁתִיָּה – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: or drank liquids not fit for drinking: he is exempt.
This implies that if they were fit, he is liable.
But why would he be liable?
He only said, "An oath that I will not eat"!
phrases.notes: Since he never mentioned drinking, being liable for drinks shows that 'eat' covers drinking too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second support from the משנה for the view that drinking is included in eating
steps.raayaObject: Drinking is included in the word 'eating' in an oath
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's exemption for undrinkable liquids implies liability for drinkable ones under an oath that mentioned only eating

steps.title: Maybe he swore separately about drinking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב אשי's proof. Maybe the person in the משנה took two oaths, one not to eat and one not to drink.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he said two oaths: 'An oath that I will not eat' and 'an oath that I will not drink.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב אשי's proof by suggesting a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he swore both not to eat and not to drink, then of course he is liable for drinkable liquids. So the משנה does not prove that 'eating' includes drinking. The proof falls away, although the view itself is not disproved.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps; opens a possibility that weakens a proof

steps.confusionAlert: This only takes away רב אשי's proof. It does not show that drinking is NOT included in eating.

phrases.english: Perhaps it is a case where he said two oaths:
"An oath that I will not eat," and "an oath that I will not drink."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 13
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the משנה, not the view itself
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה could be talking about someone who took a separate oath about drinking

steps.title: Maybe naming the breads only shuts out other foods
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the three breads. It asks: when a person names each kind of bread, maybe he only wants to leave other foods out of his oath, not to create separate oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and he ate wheat bread, and so on. But maybe, when he lists the breads, he only wants to free himself from the other foods?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It questions why listing each bread makes him liable for each one separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that if he swore not to eat wheat bread, barley bread, and spelt bread, he brings a separate קרבן for each. The challenge offers another reason for the list. Maybe he named the breads to limit the oath to them, so that other foods stay allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: To exempt himself, to keep things outside the oath

phrases.aramaic: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל, וְאָכַל פַּת חִטִּין כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: "An oath that I will not eat," and he ate wheat bread, and so on.
phrases.notes: The quote opens the משנה's case. The question is really about the next case there, where he named each bread in the oath itself.

phrases.english: But perhaps, to free himself
from the other foods is why he comes to list them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next part of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that listing each bread makes him liable for each one
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The list can be explained as limiting the oath to these breads, so it does not prove that he made separate oaths

steps.title: He could have just said wheat, barley, and spelt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: if he only wanted to leave out other foods, he could have said 'wheat, barley, and spelt.' Saying 'bread' each time shows that he meant separate oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should have said: 'wheat, barley, and spelt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to the extra words in the oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming the three grains would have been enough to limit the oath. Repeating the word 'bread' with each grain is extra wording. That extra wording shows he meant each bread as its own oath.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have said; the extra wording must have a reason

phrases.english: He should have said
"wheat, barley, and spelt."
phrases.notes: He means without repeating the word 'bread' each time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra wording shows what he meant
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing the breads only limits the oath to them
steps.terutzMaskana: Repeating 'bread' each time is extra, so it must mean separate oaths

steps.title: Maybe 'bread' was needed to rule out chewing raw grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer. If he had said only 'wheat, barley, and spelt,' it might have meant chewing the raw kernels, so he needed to say 'bread.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps he needed the word 'bread,' because otherwise the oath would mean chewing the raw grain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes apart the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'bread' could have its own purpose: to limit the oath to bread and not raw grain. If so, the word is not extra. Then it does not prove that he meant separate oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: To chew, here raw whole grain kernels

phrases.english: But perhaps, without 'bread,' the oath would mean chewing raw grain?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 16
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The answer that repeating 'bread' proves separate oaths
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word 'bread' has its own job, to limit the oath to bread and not raw grain, so it is not extra

steps.title: He could have said 'bread of wheat, barley, and spelt'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a new shorter wording. If he only wanted to limit his oath to bread, he could have said 'bread of wheat, barley, and spelt' with the word 'bread' said only once.
steps.simpleTranslation: He could have said: 'Bread of wheat, barley, and spelt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries again to prove that saying 'bread' for each grain means separate oaths. It suggests a shorter way he could have said it, with 'bread' said only once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 17 the גמרא said that 'wheat, barley, and spelt' alone might mean chewing raw kernels. So now it puts the word 'bread' at the start, one time only. If one 'bread' at the front would cover all three grains, then saying 'bread' three times must have been to make separate oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have said / he could have said

phrases.english: For he could have said:
phrases.notes: The person in the משנה could have made his oath in a shorter way, if all he wanted was to talk only about bread.

phrases.english: "Bread of wheat, barley, and spelt."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the rejection in step 17 by suggesting a new short wording that puts 'bread' at the front, so it cannot mean raw kernels.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Another possible wording: he could have said it more briefly, so the extra repetition must mean something.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Repeating 'bread' might only be there to leave other foods out of the oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: A single 'bread' at the front would already do that, so the repeated 'bread' must make separate oaths.

steps.title: That wording could mean wheat as bread, barley and spelt even raw
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. 'Bread of wheat, barley, and spelt' could be read as 'bread of wheat' for eating, and 'barley and spelt' even as raw kernels to chew.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe 'bread of wheat' means eating wheat bread, and 'barley and spelt' means chewing the raw kernels?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 18. It shows the short wording could be misunderstood, so the person had a good reason not to use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'bread' said once, it might attach only to wheat. Then 'barley and spelt' would stand alone and could forbid even chewing raw kernels, just as in step 17. So he had to repeat 'bread' to make it clear that all three are about bread, and the proof for separate oaths falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps, maybe (opens a different possible reading)

phrases.english: But perhaps "bread of wheat" means for eating,
and "barley and spelt" means for chewing?
phrases.notes: He means the word 'bread' might belong only to wheat, so barley and spelt would be forbidden even as raw grain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the short wording suggested in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the specific wording offered in step 18, not the whole idea that repeating 'bread' could be extra.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A single 'bread' might cover only wheat, leaving barley and spelt open to mean chewing raw kernels. So repeating 'bread' had a real purpose.

steps.title: He could have said 'bread of wheat, and of barley, and of spelt'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a better short wording: 'bread of wheat, and of barley, and of spelt.' The word 'of' ties each grain back to 'bread', so it clearly means only bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: He could have said: 'Bread of wheat, and of barley, and of spelt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem from step 19 by suggesting a different short wording. In this wording the word 'of' makes it clear that every grain is about bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'and of barley, and of spelt' points each grain back to the one word 'bread', so nobody could think it means chewing raw kernels. This wording would have limited the oath to bread without saying 'bread' three times. So since he did repeat 'bread', the repetition must be there to make separate oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: And of (ties the grain back to the word 'bread')

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the גמרא's strongest try to show that saying 'bread' again for each kind means a separate oath for each one. That is why the person in the משנה is liable for each bread separately.

phrases.english: For he could have said:
"Bread of wheat, and of barley, and of spelt."
phrases.notes: The little word 'of' links barley and spelt back to 'bread', so this can only mean bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר ״פַּת חִטִּין וְשֶׁל שְׂעוֹרִין וְשֶׁל כּוּסְּמִין״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the rejection in step 19 by offering a clearer short wording that cannot be read as chewing raw kernels.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A better possible wording: a clear, shorter way to limit the oath to bread existed, so repeating 'bread' must mean something extra.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Repeating 'bread' was needed so barley and spelt would not be read as raw kernels.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'And of barley, and of spelt' would have solved that, so the repeated 'bread' must make separate oaths.
